CSCN8000 – Lab 3: Supervised Learning (Logistic and Linear Regression)¶

Name: Juan Antonio Sainz Gálvez Student ID: 9072844 Section: 1 Course: CSCN8000 – Artificial Intelligence Algorithms and Mathematics, Conestoga College

This notebook contains two parts:

  • Part A – Credit card fraud detection with logistic regression (classification).
  • Part B – Insurance cost prediction with linear regression (regression).

Both parts follow the same steps: load the data, preprocess and analyse it, split it into train (0.7) and test (0.3), build the model and evaluate it.

0. Setup and configuration¶

Everything needed to run this notebook:

  1. Create the virtual environment in this folder and install the packages: run setup_lab3_env.bat (or python -m venv .venv and .venv\Scripts\pip install -r requirements_lab3.txt).
  2. Put the two Kaggle downloads in the same folder as this notebook, without unzipping them:
    • archive_card.zip → contains creditcard.csv (https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mlg-ulb/creditcardfraud)
    • archive_insurance.zip → contains insurance.csv (https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mirichoi0218/insurance)
  3. Select the .venv kernel and run all cells.

pandas reads a .zip that contains a single CSV directly, so the 150 MB CSV never has to be extracted.

In [1]:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay,
                             classification_report, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score,
                             roc_auc_score, average_precision_score,
                             r2_score, mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error)

RANDOM_STATE = 42          # same split every time the notebook runs
TEST_SIZE = 0.30           # train 0.7 / test 0.3, as the lab requires
CARD_FILE = "archive_card.zip"
INSURANCE_FILE = "archive_insurance.zip"

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.4f}")
print("Libraries loaded")

Libraries loaded

Part A – Credit Card Fraud Detection (Logistic Regression)¶

Problem statement: Consider the dataset Credit Card Fraud Detection from Kaggle and build a machine-learning model that detects whether a credit card transaction is fraudulent. Demonstrate the steps of data preprocessing and analysis, consider applying train (0.7) and test (0.3), using the logistic regression to build the model, and evaluate to determine the accuracy.

A.1 Load the data¶

The dataset has transactions made by European cardholders over two days in September 2013. V1–V28 are PCA components (already anonymised and transformed by the data owners), Time is the seconds since the first transaction, Amount is the transaction amount and Class is the target (1 = fraud, 0 = genuine).

print("Shape (rows, columns):", card.shape)

A.2 Data preprocessing – structure, missing values and duplicates¶

In [3]:
print(card.dtypes.value_counts())
print()
print("Missing values in the whole table:", card.isna().sum().sum())
print("Duplicated rows:", card.duplicated().sum())

float64    30
int64       1
Name: count, dtype: int64

Missing values in the whole table: 0

Duplicated rows: 1081

There are no missing values. The duplicated rows are exact copies (same time, same amount, same 28 components), so they add no information and could appear in both train and test, making the test look better than it is. They are removed.

In [4]:
rows_before = len(card)
card = card.drop_duplicates().reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"Rows before: {rows_before:,}  |  removed: {rows_before - len(card):,}  |  rows after: {len(card):,}")

Rows before: 284,807  |  removed: 1,081  |  rows after: 283,726

A.3 Data analysis – class balance¶

In [5]:
counts = card["Class"].value_counts().sort_index()
share = card["Class"].value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index() * 100
balance = pd.DataFrame({"transactions": counts, "percent": share.round(3)})

plt.ylabel("Number of transactions (log)")
plt.show()

             transactions  percent
Genuine (0)        283253  99.8330
Fraud (1)             473   0.1670

Finding: the data is extremely imbalanced – fewer than 2 in every 1,000 transactions are fraud. This matters for the evaluation: a "model" that always answers genuine would already reach about 99.8 % accuracy while catching zero frauds. So accuracy is reported, as requested, but precision, recall and the confusion matrix are also needed to judge the model honestly.

In [6]:
baseline_accuracy = (card["Class"] == 0).mean()
print(f"Accuracy of always predicting 'genuine': {baseline_accuracy:.4%}")

Accuracy of always predicting 'genuine': 99.8333%

Findings: half of the frauds are under about $10 (median $9.82 vs $22 for genuine transactions), although a few larger frauds raise the fraud mean to about $124; the maximum fraud is only about $2,126. The ranges overlap heavily, so Amount alone does not separate the classes. Frauds happen throughout the two days, including at night when genuine traffic is low.

Amount and Time are on very different scales from V1–V28 (which are PCA components centred near 0). Logistic regression uses gradient-based optimisation and its coefficients depend on scale, so these two columns will be standardised.

A.6 Train (0.7) / test (0.3) split and scaling¶

  • stratify=y keeps the same fraud percentage in train and test; without it the test set could get very few frauds by chance.
  • The scaler is fitted only on the training data and then applied to the test data, so no information from the test set leaks into training.
In [10]:
X = card.drop(columns="Class")
y = card["Class"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=TEST_SIZE, stratify=y, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train = X_train.copy(); X_test = X_test.copy()
X_train[["Time", "Amount"]] = scaler.fit_transform(X_train[["Time", "Amount"]])
X_test[["Time", "Amount"]] = scaler.transform(X_test[["Time", "Amount"]])

print(f"Train: {len(X_train):,} rows, frauds = {y_train.sum()} ({y_train.mean():.3%})")
print(f"Test : {len(X_test):,} rows, frauds = {y_test.sum()} ({y_test.mean():.3%})")

Train: 198,608 rows, frauds = 331 (0.167%)
Test : 85,118 rows, frauds = 142 (0.167%)

A.7 Build the logistic regression model¶

In [11]:
log_model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
log_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred_train = log_model.predict(X_train)
y_pred = log_model.predict(X_test)
y_prob = log_model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
print("Model trained")

Model trained

A.8 Evaluate – accuracy¶

In [12]:
train_acc = accuracy_score(y_train, y_pred_train)
test_acc = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)
print(f"Training accuracy : {train_acc:.4%}")
print(f"Test accuracy     : {test_acc:.4%}")
print(f"Baseline accuracy (always 'genuine'): {(y_test == 0).mean():.4%}")

Training accuracy : 99.9240%
Test accuracy     : 99.9107%
Baseline accuracy (always 'genuine'): 99.8332%

A.9 Evaluate – confusion matrix, precision, recall¶

In [13]:
cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)
ConfusionMatrixDisplay(cm, display_labels=["Genuine", "Fraud"]).plot(cmap="Blues", values_format=",")
plt.title("Logistic regression – test set")
plt.grid(False)
plt.show()

tn, fp, fn, tp = cm.ravel()
print(f"Frauds caught (true positives)       : {tp}")
print(f"Frauds missed (false negatives)      : {fn}")
print(f"Genuine flagged as fraud (false pos.): {fp}")
print(f"Genuine correctly accepted           : {tn:,}")
print()
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred, target_names=["Genuine", "Fraud"], digits=4))
print(f"ROC-AUC           : {roc_auc_score(y_test, y_prob):.4f}")
print(f"PR-AUC (avg. precision): {average_precision_score(y_test, y_prob):.4f}")

Frauds caught (true positives)       : 81
Frauds missed (false negatives)      : 61
Genuine flagged as fraud (false pos.): 15
Genuine correctly accepted           : 84,961

              precision    recall  f1-score   support

     Genuine     0.9993    0.9998    0.9996     84976
       Fraud     0.8438    0.5704    0.6807       142

    accuracy                         0.9991     85118
   macro avg     0.9215    0.7851    0.8401     85118
weighted avg     0.9990    0.9991    0.9990     85118

ROC-AUC           : 0.9650

PR-AUC (avg. precision): 0.7042

Interpretation

  • Precision (fraud): of the transactions the model flags as fraud, the share that really are fraud.
  • Recall (fraud): of all real frauds, the share the model catches. For a bank this is usually the most important number, because a missed fraud costs money.
  • ROC-AUC / PR-AUC: how well the predicted probabilities rank frauds above genuine transactions, independent of the 0.5 cut-off. PR-AUC is the more informative one for very imbalanced data.

A.10 Extra: logistic regression with balanced class weights¶

Because only ~0.17 % of the data is fraud, the default model learns mostly from genuine transactions. class_weight="balanced" makes each fraud count as much as many genuine transactions during training. This is still logistic regression; only the training weights change.

In [14]:
bal_model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced", random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
bal_model.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred_bal = bal_model.predict(X_test)

comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    "Accuracy":         [accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred),  accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred_bal)],
    "Fraud precision":  [precision_score(y_test, y_pred), precision_score(y_test, y_pred_bal)],
    "Fraud recall":     [recall_score(y_test, y_pred),    recall_score(y_test, y_pred_bal)],
    "Fraud F1":         [f1_score(y_test, y_pred),        f1_score(y_test, y_pred_bal)],
    "Frauds caught":    [int(((y_pred == 1) & (y_test == 1)).sum()), int(((y_pred_bal == 1) & (y_test == 1)).sum())],
    "False alarms":     [int(((y_pred == 1) & (y_test == 0)).sum()), int(((y_pred_bal == 1) & (y_test == 0)).sum())],
}, index=["Default logistic regression", "Balanced logistic regression"])
comparison
Out[14]:
Accuracy Fraud precision Fraud recall Fraud F1 Frauds caught False alarms
Default logistic regression 0.9991 0.8438 0.5704 0.6807 81 15
Balanced logistic regression 0.9733 0.0529 0.8873 0.0998 126 2257

cm_bal = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred_bal)
ConfusionMatrixDisplay(cm_bal, display_labels=["Genuine", "Fraud"]).plot(cmap="Oranges", values_format=",")

A.11 Part A – Conclusions¶

In [16]:
print(f"Default model  -> test accuracy {test_acc:.4%}, catches {recall_score(y_test, y_pred):.1%} of frauds, "
      f"{precision_score(y_test, y_pred):.1%} of its alerts are real frauds")
print(f"Balanced model -> test accuracy {accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred_bal):.4%}, catches {recall_score(y_test, y_pred_bal):.1%} of frauds, "
      f"{precision_score(y_test, y_pred_bal):.1%} of its alerts are real frauds")

Default model  -> test accuracy 99.9107%, catches 57.0% of frauds, 84.4% of its alerts are real frauds
Balanced model -> test accuracy 97.3296%, catches 88.7% of frauds, 5.3% of its alerts are real frauds
  1. After removing duplicates and standardising Time and Amount, a logistic regression trained on 70 % of the data reaches a test accuracy of 99.91 % (training 99.92 %), so it is not overfitting.
  2. Accuracy alone is misleading here: always predicting "genuine" already gives about 99.8 %. The real value of the model is shown by the confusion matrix: the default model catches 81 of 142 frauds (57 %), and 84 % of its alerts are real frauds (only 15 false alarms out of 85,118 test transactions). ROC-AUC is 0.965.
  3. With balanced class weights the model catches 126 of 142 frauds (89 %), but raises 2,257 false alarms and accuracy drops to 97.3 %. Which version is better is a business decision: the cost of a missed fraud versus the cost of reviewing or blocking a genuine transaction.

Part B – Insurance Cost Prediction (Linear Regression)¶

Problem statement: Use the following insurance dataset and build a predictive system to predict insurance costs. Demonstrate the steps of data preprocessing and analysis, consider applying train (0.7) and test (0.3), using linear regression to build the model, and evaluate the accuracy of predicting the insurance cost.

Findings

  • Smoking is by far the strongest factor: smokers pay roughly 3–4 times more than non-smokers.
  • Charges grow steadily with age, in three visible bands (non-smokers, smokers, and smokers with high BMI).
  • BMI matters mainly for smokers: smokers with BMI above 30 form the highest-cost group.
  • Sex and region make only small differences.

B.5 Preprocessing – encode categorical columns¶

One-hot encoding turns each category into a 0/1 column. drop_first=True drops one category per column (it becomes the reference), which avoids redundant columns that would make the linear regression coefficients unstable.

B.7 Build the linear regression model¶

In [29]:
lin_model = LinearRegression()
lin_model.fit(Xi_train, yi_train)

coef = pd.Series(lin_model.coef_, index=X_ins.columns).sort_values(ascending=False)
print(f"Intercept: ${lin_model.intercept_:,.0f}")
print("\nChange in yearly charges for a one-unit increase in each feature (others held constant):")
for name, value in coef.items():
    print(f"  {name:<18} {value:>+12,.0f} USD")

Intercept: $-11,517

Change in yearly charges for a one-unit increase in each feature (others held constant):
  smoker_yes              +22,874 USD
  children                   +522 USD
  bmi                        +328 USD
  age                        +251 USD
  sex_male                   -112 USD
  region_northwest           -466 USD
  region_southwest           -766 USD
  region_southeast           -936 USD

Reading the coefficients: being a smoker adds about $22,900 a year**, each extra year of age adds about **$250, each extra BMI point about $330** and each child about **$520, holding the other features constant. Sex (about −$110) and region (a few hundred dollars) have small effects.

B.8 Evaluate – how accurate are the predicted costs?¶

For a regression model "accuracy" is measured with:

  • R² (coefficient of determination): share of the variation in charges explained by the model (1.0 = perfect).
  • MAE (mean absolute error): on average, how many dollars the prediction is off.
  • RMSE (root mean squared error): like MAE but penalises large errors more.
In [30]:
yi_pred_train = lin_model.predict(Xi_train)
yi_pred = lin_model.predict(Xi_test)

metrics = pd.DataFrame({
    "R²":        [r2_score(yi_train, yi_pred_train), r2_score(yi_test, yi_pred)],
    "MAE (USD)": [mean_absolute_error(yi_train, yi_pred_train), mean_absolute_error(yi_test, yi_pred)],
    "RMSE (USD)":[np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(yi_train, yi_pred_train)), np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(yi_test, yi_pred))],
}, index=["Train (70%)", "Test (30%)"])

The points follow the diagonal for most people, but the residual plot shows patterns instead of random noise: the model under-predicts some high-cost people (mainly smokers with high BMI). A straight-line model cannot fully capture the "smoker × BMI" effect seen in B.4.

B.9 Predictive system – estimate the cost for a new person¶

In [33]:
def predict_insurance_cost(age, sex, bmi, children, smoker, region):
    """Return the predicted yearly insurance charges (USD) for one person."""
    person = pd.DataFrame([{"age": age, "sex": sex, "bmi": bmi, "children": children,
                            "smoker": smoker, "region": region}])
    person = pd.get_dummies(person, columns=["sex", "smoker", "region"], dtype=int)
    person = person.reindex(columns=X_ins.columns, fill_value=0)   # same columns as training
    return float(lin_model.predict(person)[0])

examples = [
    (30, "male",   25.0, 0, "no",  "northwest"),
    (30, "male",   25.0, 0, "yes", "northwest"),
    (50, "female", 32.0, 2, "no",  "southeast"),
    (50, "female", 32.0, 2, "yes", "southeast"),
]
for age, sex, bmi, children, smoker, region in examples:
    cost = predict_insurance_cost(age, sex, bmi, children, smoker, region)
    print(f"Age {age}, {sex}, BMI {bmi}, {children} children, smoker={smoker}, {region}: "
          f"predicted ${cost:,.0f} per year")

B.10 Part B – Conclusions¶

In [34]:
print(f"Test R²  : {r2_score(yi_test, yi_pred):.3f}  -> the model explains about {r2_score(yi_test, yi_pred):.0%} of the variation in charges")
print(f"Test MAE : ${mean_absolute_error(yi_test, yi_pred):,.0f}  -> average error per person per year")
print(f"Test RMSE: ${np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(yi_test, yi_pred)):,.0f}")

Test R²  : 0.772  -> the model explains about 77% of the variation in charges
Test MAE : $4,182  -> average error per person per year
Test RMSE: $6,240
  1. After removing one duplicate and one-hot encoding sex, smoker and region, a linear regression trained on 70 % of the data explains 77 % of the variation in insurance charges on the unseen 30 % test set (R² = 0.772).
  2. Train and test scores are close (R² 0.736 vs 0.772), so the model is not overfitting.
  3. Smoking, age and BMI drive the cost; sex and region matter very little.
  4. The average error is about **$4,180 per person per year** (RMSE about $6,240), with the largest errors on smokers with high BMI. A natural next step would be adding an interaction feature (smoker × BMI) or a non-linear model, but the lab asks for plain linear regression, which already gives a useful first estimate.
